transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (Quantaco Head of ML), Liam Chen (Quantaco Infra), Priya Das (Quantaco Product)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC check-in — cost/econ review. Focus on tokens per second per dollar, caching and batching tradeoffs, and next benchmark steps.

[00:00] Sam Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick check — agenda is cost/unit economics, runbook on the benchmark Jordan ran last week, and next steps. Maya, Liam, Priya, you good with that?
[00:10] Maya Ortiz: Yep, good.
[00:12] Liam Chen: All good.
[00:15] Jordan Lee: Quick note — I posted the raw logs in the shared drive, link in the chat. There are two runs: hosted (Redwood-hosted standard) and dedicated with 4 workers, quantized int8 variant.
[00:25] Priya Das: We skimmed the sheet this morning, some numbers looked promising but we had questions on the assumptions.

[02:00] Sam Patel: Right. High level numbers first — for the quantized int8 70B run on dedicated we saw ~1,200 tokens/sec at peak, cost per 1M tokens about $2.10 given reserved pricing assumptions. On hosted with the same quantized model and default batching we saw ~900 tokens/sec and $2.80 per 1M. Those are rough.
[02:30] Maya Ortiz: That delta is helpful. Curious about how caching affected those numbers — Jordan, you had a prefix cache experiment?
[02:45] Jordan Lee: Yeah. With prefix KV caching enabled (we cached repeated system prompts and common starter context) we saw effective tokens emitted per dollar increase by ~2.4x on our chat workload. The raw tokens/sec didn't change dramatically — throughput improved modestly to ~1,350 tokens/sec on dedicated for the happy path because caching avoids recompute for early token generation. But effective downstream token cost drops since many tokens are served from cache.
[03:20] Liam Chen: When you say 'effective' tokens, is that counting cache hits as zero compute? Because our billing model will still count inbound/outbound HTTP traffic.
[03:35] Jordan Lee: Good point. For the sheet we counted compute token-equivalents: cache-hit tokens were excluded from compute time. We also added an overhead line for transfer and small egress but that's <5% in our test. We can add a column with cache-hit billing impact if you want.

[05:00] Maya Ortiz: Also concerned about quality degradation with quantization. Did you compare outputs side-by-side?
[05:12] Jordan Lee: We did a quick eval on the prompt set Maya provided. Quantized int8 preserved quality for the majority of prompts; we flagged about 4% regressions on specificity metrics for the most knowledge-intensive prompts. We recommend keeping an evaluation guardrail set and configuring fallback to a higher-precision variant for those trigger prompts.
[05:45] Priya Das: That's reasonable. For product, predictability matters more than tiny cost wins if it impacts NPS.

[07:00] Sam Patel: Let's talk batching tradeoffs. Jordan?
[07:05] Jordan Lee: Sure. Increasing batch size from 1 to 8 improved tokens/sec significantly — dedicated: from ~1,200 to ~3,400 tokens/sec peak — but median latency per request climbed from ~60ms to ~240ms. For chat product UX that can be noticeable for short-turn interactions. The sweet spot heaviest for you depends on session distribution — if you have many long-turn sessions batching helps; for low-turn interactive, keep lower batches and rely on caching.
[07:50] Liam Chen: Our sessions average 4 turns with a lot of short queries, so increasing latency to 240ms might be visible. Do you have a breakdown of p95 latency at batch size 4?
[08:05] Jordan Lee: Yes — batch size 4 gave ~1,900 tokens/sec and p95 latency ~120-150ms. So tradeoff middle ground.

[09:30] Maya Ortiz: On dedicated vs hosted cost — aside from raw tokens/sec, what about reserved commit amortization? We need monthly forecasts.
[09:45] Sam Patel: In the sheet I modeled three buckets: on-demand hosted, dedicated reserved (monthly commit), and hybrid with burst to hosted. Reserved flips favorably when steady-state QPS is above ~750 tokens/sec sustained. The break-even depends on utilization — at 70% utilization reserved is ~30% cheaper than hosted for your mix.
[10:15] Priya Das: Is that assuming no caching?
[10:20] Sam Patel: It's base compute only. Caching benefits reduce compute consumption, which can make reserved less favourable if bursts drop — but if caching reduces compute costs across the board, it lowers absolute spend and still keeps dedicated attractive because you get more throughput per-dollar. We'll add a calc for reserved effective cost after cache.

[12:00] Liam Chen: What about autoscaling and sudden spikes? We worry about cold-start latency for added workers. In our load tests a 3x traffic spike happened and we want <500ms degradation.
[12:18] Jordan Lee: Autoscale policy config we suggested uses fast warm-up with buffer headroom — maintain one warm standby worker per shard. Cold-start for a new GPU instance is the problem if you provision from zero, but Redwood supports burst to hosted in those windows — you can route overflow to hosted API to maintain latency SLA. That will increase cost during spikes but preserve UX.
[12:52] Maya Ortiz: Any numbers on cost for overflow? If we route 20% of requests to hosted during peaks, how does that affect unit economics?
[13:05] Sam Patel: Quick back-of-envelope: if 20% runs on hosted at $2.80 per 1M tokens and 80% on dedicated effective $1.80 per 1M (after reserve), blended cost becomes ~$2.04 per 1M. So modest bump. Exact depends on model variant and quantization.

[14:30] Priya Das: We saw in the logs a lot of repeated user housekeeping prompts at session start. Is there a straightforward way to cache those server-side to save tokens?
[14:42] Jordan Lee: Yes — prefix caching for common system prompts and repeated initial context is low-risk; you can treat those as immutable cache keys. We also support per-route caching TTLs and partial KV caching for longer contexts. That alone in our test cut compute by ~45% on the chat demo.
[15:10] Maya Ortiz: That aligns with our product pattern.

[17:00] Liam Chen: A couple of infra questions — network egress and encryption overhead when using private deployment vs hosted?
[17:10] Sam Patel: Hosted keeps egress within our cloud footprint, but for private (VPC) you'd manage egress and KMS. In our cost model we add a 3-5% overhead for encryption and networking; if you're on-prem the numbers change more. We'll annotate the sheet with an "infra overhead" line for private deployment.

[19:00] Jordan Lee: Another datapoint — quantization to int8 reduces GPU memory and allows more parallelism per instance so workers/sec rises. But for some prompts we saw tokenization edge cases causing slight token count differences (transcription mismatch sometimes). So include a quality margin in the model.

[21:30] Maya Ortiz: How confident are you in the tokens/sec numbers? Are they steady-state or bursts?
[21:40] Jordan Lee: The published numbers are peak sustained over a 5-minute window in our benchmark. Steady-state average is ~10-15% lower. We included p95/p99 columns in the log dump.

[23:00] Priya Das: For product decisions we need clear SLOs: cost per 1M tokens target and p95 latency target. We propose: target $2.25 per 1M and p95 <200ms for typical interactions. How close are we?
[23:20] Sam Patel: With the quantized dedicated config plus prefix caching, blended cost in the sheet is around $1.90 per 1M and p95 at ~140ms if you keep batching moderate (batch size 4) and enable warm standbys. So you are within target on both.

[25:00] Maya Ortiz: Great. Can you walk us through the exact benchmark Jordan will run? We want to reproduce locally.
[25:10] Jordan Lee: Sure. Steps: 1) use the quantized Llama-2-70B int8 artifact we uploaded, 2) configure 4 workers per shard, 3) enable prefix KV cache with TTL 24h, 4) batch size 4, rate limit 1,000 concurrent tokens across cluster, 5) run for 60 minutes capturing p50/p95/p99 and cache hit ratio. I'll push the script and infra.tf in the shared folder.
[26:05] Liam Chen: When you say cache hit ratio, what's a realistic number?
[26:12] Jordan Lee: In our chat dataset we saw ~37% cache-hit for initial prompt patterns; for more templated flows it was 50-60%. We'll report both overall and per-route.

[28:00] Priya Das: Any legal or compliance notes about caching user content? We need to make sure caching doesn't persist PII unintentionally.
[28:10] Sam Patel: Good flag. Redwood supports configurable TTLs and explicit route-level cache rules. You can opt out for routes that might contain PII. We'll include our caching best-practices doc and config template.

[30:00] Maya Ortiz: Back to cost — can you show sensitivity to quantization hit-rate and cache hit-rate?
[30:10] Sam Patel: Yep. In the spreadsheet I added a sensitivity table: if cache hit-rate is 20% effective compute drops by ~20% and cost per 1M drops from $1.90 to ~$1.52. If you also move to int4 for select routes (where quality is acceptable) additional 18-25% savings are realistic but with higher risk.

[32:00] Liam Chen: We're cautious on int4 right now; maybe pilot on lower-risk responses only.

[33:00] Jordan Lee: Another note — batching has diminishing returns beyond 8 for your workload because turn lengths are short. So we recommend 4 as the operational default and burst to 8 during known high-throughput windows with UX caveats.

[35:00] Priya Das: For the roadmap, what's the minimal onboarding to get us from POC to pilot?
[35:10] Sam Patel: Minimal: finalize model variant(s) to use, run the Jordan benchmark and confirm tokens/sec/$, agree reserved commit sizing for dedicated (or start with hybrid), and sign off on route-level cache rules and quality guardrails. That's basically the four items.

[37:20] Maya Ortiz: Does Redwood provide tooling to continuously monitor tokens/sec/$? We want dashboards per-route and per-model.
[37:30] Jordan Lee: Yes — Redwood Console provides per-route token and cost breakdown, cost attribution, and alerts on quality regressions tied to eval sets. We can give access to a demo org retention window.

[39:00] Liam Chen: A quick question — during the benchmark will logs include per-token timings (KV lookup vs compute)? That would help us validate cache speedup assumptions.
[39:12] Jordan Lee: Yes, logs include timing decomposition: KV lookup vs attention compute vs kernel time. We also include tokenized counts and network overhead.

[41:00] Priya Das: Ok last part — next steps recap?
[41:10] Sam Patel: Recap: Jordan will run the 1-hour benchmark with KV prefix cache enabled and share logs (due 2026-08-09). Sam will update and share the cost model including cache and reserved amortization (due 2026-08-06). Maya to share sample production traces and priority prompts (due 2026-08-07). We'll aim to schedule autoscale sizing deep-dive week of 2026-08-12.

[42:30] Maya Ortiz: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[42:35] Liam Chen: Thanks.
[42:38] Jordan Lee: I'll follow up in the doc.
[42:45] Sam Patel: Appreciate it. We'll email the artifacts and next steps.

Transcript notes: occasional transcription artifacts — e.g., "K V" for KV, "int eight" for int8, some proper names garbled. Links shared: drive/logs/quantaco/benchmark-0805, docs/redwood/cache-best-practices.pdf.

End of meeting.
